input: It is worth noting that the phase behaviour of a partially miscible liquid pair can, in many respects, be understood as a rich and intricate interplay between molecular interactions and thermodynamic constraints, and this interplay ultimately governs whether a given mixture will remain as a single homogeneous liquid or will instead split into separate layers. Essentially, when two liquids are only partially miscible, the system does not behave in a simple, uniform way across the whole composition range; rather, over part of that range, the mixture separates into two distinct liquid phases that coexist side by side. The fundamental criterion that underlies this behaviour, before any equation is even named, can be expressed in words: the chemical potential of each component must be equal across the phases at equilibrium. In other words, equilibrium is not simply a matter of concentrations looking balanced; it is the deeper condition that no component has any tendency to migrate from one phase to the other. Each layer is rich in one component and comparatively poor in the other, and the composition of each layer is dictated by this equality condition rather than by the overall composition that was originally charged to the vessel. Overall, the picture that emerges is that partial miscibility reflects an underlying balance, and the equilibrium condition expressed in words — equality of chemical potential across the phases — is the central idea that ties the whole description together, highlighting how the two liquid layers can coexist in a stable and reproducible manner.
target:
Phase equilibrium for a partially miscible liquid pair rests on a condition stated in words before any equation is named: at fixed temperature and pressure, the chemical potential of each component is equal in the two liquid phases. Equality of chemical potential is required for every component at the same time, and a component whose chemical potential differed between the phases would pass from one phase to the other until the difference vanished.

Partial miscibility confines the separation to part of the composition range. Inside that range the mixture forms two layers, each rich in one liquid and holding the other as the minor part. Layer compositions are set by the equilibrium condition, not by the overall charge: a change in overall composition inside the range changes the amounts of the layers, while each layer keeps its equilibrium composition at that temperature. Outside the range the pair is a single liquid and no layer equilibrium arises.

Equilibrium for the pair is therefore a statement about the layers themselves. Their compositions, and the boundary of the range over which they form, follow from equality of chemical potential across the phases together with the material balance on each component. The passage is conceptual: no measured data are introduced, and quantitative layer compositions require activity data or measurements on the actual pair.
